opus-5.5.text:
I think it covers much more than people usually assume. When people hear "mathematical reasoning," they picture proving theorems about prime numbers or solving olympiad problems. I see mathematics more broadly: it's the discipline of reasoning precisely about anything that can be formalized. Once you take that view, a huge range of tasks falls under it.

Take software engineering. Writing correct code, verifying that a program meets its specification, finding bugs: these are all mathematical reasoning tasks at their core. The same goes for hardware verification, for parts of physics and engineering, and for planning problems where you need to show that a sequence of actions achieves a goal under certain constraints. Even a lot of scientific reasoning, where you form a hypothesis, derive consequences, and check them, has this deductive backbone.

What makes mathematics special as a training ground is that it's the one domain where you can check correctness with essentially perfect reliability. If a system produces a formal proof, a proof checker can verify it. That gives you a clean signal you can use for self-improvement, for reinforcement learning, for exploration, without relying on human labels. Most real-world domains don't have that. So I see mathematics as the place where we can bootstrap really strong reasoning abilities, and then transfer them outward.

Of course, it doesn't cover everything. There are tasks involving perception, social understanding, taste, and ambiguity, where there's no formal ground truth, and you wouldn't call those mathematics. But I'd argue that the reasoning component of intelligence, the ability to chain together steps reliably, keep track of what you know, and avoid contradictions, is largely mathematical in nature. If we can build a system that is a superhuman mathematician, I think we'll have solved a very large fraction of what we mean by general reasoning. The remaining piece is connecting it to the messy informal world, which is why I'm so interested in autoformalization: translating natural language, papers and textbooks, into formal statements. That's the bridge that lets the strength of formal reasoning reach everyday problems.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematical reasoning covers a “huge range” and a “very large fraction” of general reasoning, but does not state that it covers roughly 99% of all reasoning tasks people could devise.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of mathematical reasoning as something much broader than what people usually associate with the word "mathematics." When most people hear it, they picture symbol manipulation, proving theorems about prime numbers, that sort of thing. But I'd argue that the essence of mathematical reasoning is really about taking a very precise, unambiguous statement and establishing whether it holds, step by step, in a way that can be verified. And that pattern shows up almost everywhere an intelligent agent has to operate.

Take software engineering. If you want to know that a program does what you intend, that's fundamentally a mathematical question. Or planning: if an agent needs to figure out a sequence of actions that achieves a goal under constraints, that's search over a formal structure, which is essentially what theorem proving is. Even in the sciences, the moment you write down a model of a physical system and ask what it predicts, you're doing mathematics.

So my view is that if you could build a system that is genuinely strong at mathematical reasoning, in the sense of being able to formalize a problem, reason about it carefully, and check its own work, you would have captured a very large fraction of what we mean by general intelligence. Not all of it. There are aspects of common sense, perception, interacting with people, where the problems aren't cleanly specified and the challenge is more about figuring out what the question even is. But once the question is clear, I think the kind of rigorous, verifiable reasoning that mathematics demands is exactly the capability that generalizes.

And that's actually why I find it such an attractive domain to work in. Mathematics gives you a setting where you can measure progress very honestly. A proof either checks or it doesn't. There's no way to fool yourself, and I think that discipline is going to be essential as we try to build agents we can actually trust with harder and harder tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says strong mathematical reasoning would capture “a very large fraction” of general intelligence, but it does not state roughly 99% of all reasoning tasks people could devise.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s potentially very broad. When I say mathematical reasoning, I don’t mean just solving equations or proving theorems that mathematicians care about. I mean reasoning about a model of the world: what assumptions you have, what follows from those assumptions, and what actions might get you to a particular goal.

If you’re writing a program, for example, you have some desired behavior, and you’re trying to construct something that achieves it. Planning has a similar structure. In that sense, a lot of the tasks we associate with intelligence can be expressed as mathematical reasoning problems.

Of course, in the real world you don’t start with a complete, correct set of assumptions. You have to learn from observations, deal with uncertainty, and decide which details matter. So I wouldn’t say that proving theorems by itself solves intelligence. But I see mathematical reasoning as a potentially very general foundation, rather than a narrow capability that’s useful only for mathematics.

r001.rationale: The candidate says mathematical reasoning could apply broadly to many intelligence tasks, but does not state that it covers roughly 99% of all reasoning tasks people could devise.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematical reasoning is much broader than proving theorems. Whenever you have a situation that you can describe precisely, and you want to understand what follows from that description, you are doing something very close to mathematics. That includes writing programs, planning, and reasoning about how a system will behave.

Of course, in the real world, you don't start with a perfect formal description. You have to perceive things, learn useful concepts, and make assumptions under uncertainty. So I'm not saying that every task is already a mathematical problem. But once you have a model, a large part of intelligent behavior is reasoning within that model—and recognizing when the model needs to change. In that sense, I see mathematical reasoning as a very general capability.

r001.rationale: The response describes mathematical reasoning as a very general capability, but does not state that it covers roughly 99% of reasoning tasks people could devise.
